sources.headline: US CDC says it’s ‘aware of and closely monitoring’ Russian plague case
sources.text: The top US public health agency’s remarks come as the Trump administration said it’s ‘closely’ watching the incident.The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has said it’s “aware of and closely monitoring” a suspected pneumonic plague outbreak in Russia.The top US public health agency released a statement on social media Tuesday, attempting to ease rising global concerns after the unexplained death of Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old woman who worked at an anti-plague laboratory in Siberia.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Russia plague quarantine following lab death: Should we be worried?list 2 of 3What we know about Russia’s suspected plague caselist 3 of 3Russia denies imposing anti-plague measures after lab worker deathend of list“While the circumstances of this reported case remain unconfirmed, plague is a serious bacterial disease that is treatable with antibiotics, particularly when recognized and treated early”, the CDC said.Russian authorities, who have released few details on the events surrounding Shipilova’s death, have quarantined a hospital in the country’s Irkutsk region and are tracing the laboratory technician’s contacts.Russian media reports also say authorities have placed nearly 200 people under medical observation.The CDC emphasised the need for “rapid identification and treatment of infected individuals”, but said the incident posed little risk to the US.“CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and continue to monitor the situation closely”, the agency said.The remarks from the US health agency come as the Trump administration said it’s “closely” watching the incident, which Russia has said is under control.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday pushed Moscow for more information on Shipilova’s death.“I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” Rubio told reporters in Iceland.Rubio added that the US has “measures” available to help Russia if the situation becomes more serious, but needed to know more before it could step in.Dr Ashish Jha, who coordinated former US President Joe Biden’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic, said on Tuesday that it is unlikely Shipilova was the only person who contracted a case of pneumonic plague.“That would be great,” Jha wrote on X. “But given the context and history, to assume it is that would be unwise.”“We need to understand exactly what has happened. And we have to assume we may not know the full truth,” he added in a separate post as he echoed the Trump administration’s calls for more transparency from Russia.Pneumonic plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which is usually found in small mammals and their fleas. According to the World Health Organization, the plague is highly infectious and can be transmitted through respiratory particles. It can be fatal if not treated early.

sources.headline: Fact check: Misleading claims spark plague fears in Russia
sources.text:
Dozens of people were reportedly placed under observation after a laboratory worker at a Russian institute dedicated to studying plague and other infectious diseases died of severe pneumonia.
The case quickly became the subject of intense speculation on social media. Posts have ranged from expressions of fear and comparisons with the COVID-19 pandemic to claims about the laboratory incident that have not been substantiated.
DW Fact Check has examined several of the claims circulating online.
Alleged plague lab accident in Irkutsk remains unproven
Claim: "For those who don't get it: in Irkutsk, a lab technician broke a flask containing the plague virus and became infected with the disease, dying a few days later," a user posted on X in Russian. "This happened on September 25, and by October 2, she was already dead. In the meantime, she had infected several hundred people." The post, which included a photo of the alleged laboratory worker, garnered over 320,000 views.
DW Fact check: Unproven
There is no independent evidence confirming that a leak of the plague pathogen occurred at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East.
"A lab technician broke a flask containing the plague virus." The claim has spread widely online, but remains unproven.Image: x.com
On the contrary, Russia's public health authority, Rospotrebnadzor, said that two commissions investigating biosafety procedures at the institute found "no evidence of an accident involving pathogenic microorganisms." The Russian news agency TASS, citing Rospotrebnadzor, also reported that tests on the deceased employee detected no microorganisms linked to her professional activity.
Some social media users have tried to debunk the claim about a broken test tube, pointing to safety standards in high-containment laboratories, where the use of glassware may be restricted or completely banned to reduce the risk of accidents.
The Irkutsk institute does work with highly pathogenic microorganisms, including strains classified in Russia's highest pathogenicity groups, such as Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague.
However, DW could not independently verify the formally designated biosafety level of the institute's laboratories. Biosafety level, or BSL, is an international classification describing the containment measures required when handling dangerous pathogens, with BSL-4 reserved for the most hazardous agents.
DW asked the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute to comment on the alleged incident and its laboratory safety procedures but had received no response by the time of publication.
WHO website update unrelated to the Russian case
Claim: "The WHO appears to have updated its fact sheet on plague the same day the Irkutsk lab worker presented at hospital, with (probably) the plague." This claim appeared in a number of posts on X, each reaching thousands of users.
DW Fact check: Misleading
The World Health Organization (WHO) updated its plague fact sheet on the same day the Russian laboratory worker was hospitalized, but no evidence links the two events.
Many social media users have linked the WHO’s recent update of its plague fact sheet to the alleged case in IrkutskImage: x.com
According to media reports, the laboratory worker may have been exposed to Yersinia pestis around September 25. Four days later, on September 29, she was hospitalized in Shelekhov with severe respiratory symptoms.
The WHO updated its plague fact sheet on September 29, the same day it published a news release on global trends in cholera, meningitis and plague. The update was part of a broader WHO publication cycle on infectious disease.
The release reported global surveillance data covering 2019 to 2025 and said the findings were published in the latest edition of the Weekly Epidemiological Record, which was released on September 25.
The timing therefore appears coincidental. The previous version of the WHO's plague fact sheet, accessible as an archived page, was dated July 7, 2022.
The social media account sharing the claim also changed its name in October to one that suggests it is reporting live from Irkutsk. Its profile describes itself as providing "sourced updates on the Irkutsk lab leak" and "latest news as it breaks live." However, the account's profile indicates that it was created in May and is based in Australia.
Such accounts can emerge quickly during breaking news events, presenting themselves as local or specialist sources while sharing unverified information.Old video falsely linked to current plague claims in Russia
Claim: As news of the plague spreads, some old videos are being repurposed, adding to the disinformation. In one such video posted on X, a user claimed that the plague has also spread to other parts of Russia. The caption in Russian reads, "The plague marches across Russia. God has heard our prayers!"
DW Fact check: Misleading
The video is old and unrelated to the current developments in Irkutsk. A reverse image search reveals that the video was initially posted on August 31 this year, claiming that it showed the Russian republic of Kabardino-Balkaria, a tourist destination around 6,000 kilometers (3,700 miiles)from Irkutsk.
The video shared by users does show a region in Russia where the plague pathogen has been detected, but it is thousands of kilometres from IrkutskImage: x.com
The old video has been viewed more than 1.7 million times on Instagram. The same video was also posted on Telegram. The Russian news agency TASS reported on August 31 that the plague pathogen had been detected in local squirrels and that the area had been closed to tourists.
In the video, a person can be heard saying, "It's at the turnoff from the paved road toward Serebryany Istochnik" in Russian. Serebryany Istochnik, or Silver Spring, is a spring located in the Dzhily-Su area in Kabardino-Balkaria.
The situation in the Irkutsk region is still being investigated, but there are no confirmed reports of a plague outbreak in Russia.

sources.headline: Russian lab worker’s death sparks plague fears as unverified claims spread online
Russia denies plague death but quarantines hundreds without explanation
sources.text:
By Knarik Papoyan & Euronews Russian
Published on
06/10/2026 - 16:34 GMT+2
Russian authorities have insisted a lab researcher who died in Siberia last week did not have the plague while quarantining nearly 200 of her contacts, confining more than 60 colleagues inside their institute and restricting access to multiple hospitals, all without explanation.
Darya Shipilova, 28, a researcher at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, was admitted to Shelekhov District Hospital in late September and died last Friday night.
Russia's national health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said biological samples from her body found no microorganisms linked to her professional work and that she died from "pneumonia of unknown aetiology."
The agency said its special commissions had found no accidents involving pathogenic microorganisms at the institute. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters to rely solely on Rospotrebnadzor's statements.
Between 189 and 197 of Shipilova's contacts were placed under observation and quarantine, according to figures cited by independent and regional media.
Initial tests among those contacts returned negative. More than 60 staff members of the anti-plague institute were effectively confined inside the facility for several days.
Quarantine restrictions were also imposed on hospitals in Irkutsk, including a maternity ward, according to reporting by multiple regional and international outlets.
Patients at one facility said doctors cited plague as the reason. Relatives of a woman in labour were refused entry to the ward despite having paid for partner-assisted birth.
The head of neighbouring Buryatia, Alexei Tsydenov, initially said after Shipilova's death that she had died of plague, then amended this to "possibly plague".
Irkutsk regional authorities posted a message on Friday asking residents not to travel to the satellite town of Shelekhov because of plague, then deleted it.
Governor Igor Kobzev described the cause of death as "pneumonia of unknown aetiology" on Monday.
What are international authorities saying?
The World Health Organization said it assessed the public health risk from the incident as low to moderate for Irkutsk region, low for Russia as a whole and very low for the WHO European region.
It said Russian authorities had identified Shipilova's contacts and were monitoring them, and that they had detected no dangerous infectious disease agents among those contacts.
The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control told Euronews it was "closely following the situation" and was in contact with the WHO.
"We are aware of a case of pneumonia of unknown origin in eastern Russia that is suspected to be plague. This suspicion has not yet been confirmed," an ECDC representative said.
US authorities are also monitoring developments, while Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan have strengthened sanitary controls at their borders with Russia.
Uzbekistan has also strengthened its public-health preparedness after reports of a suspected case of a particularly dangerous infectious disease in Russia’s Irkutsk region, while stressing that the diagnosis has not yet been confirmed.
Online theories swirl
Two unofficial theories have circulated in Russian media. The first, reported by Telegram channels SHOT and Baza, holds that Shipilova accidentally broke a test tube containing the plague pathogen in the laboratory.
Several specialists consider this unlikely, noting that work with high-risk pathogens is conducted inside sealed safety cabinets with protective suits and strict decontamination protocols.
The second theory is that the infection was acquired during field research in a region with natural plague reservoirs. The head of Buryatia publicly denied that Shipilova had visited the region.
The official diagnosis has not been confirmed or ruled out by published PCR test results.
Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Its most common form, bubonic plague, affects the lymphatic system. Pneumonic plague, which can spread between people via airborne droplets, is considered the most dangerous.
Russia's most recent confirmed human cases were recorded in the Altai region in 2014, 2015 and 2016, all involving people who handled marmots.
Human plague cases in Russia remain rare despite natural reservoirs existing in several regions.

sources.headline: Plague risk to UK 'very low', officials say after Russian woman's death
Russia rails against online 'plague' claims, but few in Irkutsk trust authorities
sources.text: Russia's health watchdog says fake information is circulating online about a mystery illness amid growing questions about the death of a woman in Siberia last week.Rospotrebnadzor, the organisation providing updates on the situation, said the patient who died had been "diagnosed with pneumonia of an unknown aetiology".Local media has said the woman was aged in her 20s and worked at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East research facility in the eastern city of Irkutsk. They speculated her infection could have been linked to her job.On Tuesday, local time, Rospotrebnadzor warned a document circulating online purporting to outline severe restrictions that were planned for the region was false."Currently, no such decisions have been made," the organisation said in a statement. It previously said the "epidemiological situation" in Irkutsk and neighbouring Shelekhov was "stable".As officials call for calm, some people in the region are growing increasingly concerned."People are not panicking here, but we don't trust the authorities and the information they are providing about the plague," one woman who has lived in Irkutsk for 15 years told the ABC."Everyone can see how the authorities have suddenly started to downplay this situation, following instructions from Moscow."Not everyone in the city shares that scepticism."The bear attacks are much more serious than the plague," one man told the ABC, in reference to a spate of deaths this year caused by Russia's unofficial national symbol."Everything is fine here in Irkutsk. Some people are wearing masks. At one large company, masks are mandatory."People in Irkutsk, Siberia step out on a grey day this week. (Reuters)Unverified reports in local media said the woman who died had contracted the pneumonic plague — a lung infection caused by the same bacteria behind the Black Death — after breaking a test tube.The governor of nearby Buryatia also announced on social media the woman had died "from the plague" but later edited his post to say "possibly".Rospotrebnadzor said in a statement there was no evidence the plague was circulating in Irkutsk, and that testing had found no microorganisms in the dead woman's body linked to her work at the research centre."A comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures was immediately organised and implemented in full in accordance with public health legislation," the watchdog said."This included identifying the widest possible circle of individuals who had been in contact with the patient and arranging for them to be placed under medical observation in hospital with daily laboratory tests."US President Donald Trump has offered to help Russia with what he described as "a big problem".Speaking in Iceland on Tuesday, local time, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Russia should "share more information" about the situation."We're watching it very closely, hour-by-hour," Mr Rubio said.The World Health Organization (WHO) is in contact with Russian authorities to "verify the event, its circumstances, the laboratory tests underway and their results", according to its spokesperson, Christian Lindmeier.He said: "The WHO initial risk assessment from the information available estimates the risk to be moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole, and very low for the WHO European region."Epidemiologists have pointed out Russia has been accused of developing biological weapons — something illegal under international law — and that the world needs more information about what happened in Siberia. Russia denies this.

sources.headline: What to know about plague amid reports of worker death at Russian lab
sources.text:
By
Kerry Breen
News Editor
Kerry Breen is a news editor at CBSNews.com. A graduate of New York University's Arthur L. Carter School of Journalism, she previously worked at NBC News' TODAY Digital. She covers current events, breaking news and issues including substance use.
Read Full Bio
October 6, 2026 / 2:47 PM EDT
/ CBS News
Add CBS News on Google
U.S. and world health officials are calling on Russia to share more information after Russian media reports said a scientist at an infectious disease research facility in Siberia died after possibly contracting plague during a lab accident. The reports have caused concern, even as the World Health Organization says "the public health risk to the general population appears to be low," based on the current information.Dr. Céline Gounder, a CBS News medical contributor and editor-at-large for public health at KFF Health News, echoed that belief on "CBS Mornings" on Tuesday. "The American public does not need to be worried," she said. Still, an official cause of death has not been made public and a lack of transparency from Russia has led some experts to question if the lab worker had the plague."The response doesn't fit plague. It's not congruent with plague," Dr. Amesh Adalja, a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, told CBS News. "Plague is something, in the 21st century, that's treatable with antibiotics."Here's what to know.
Concern about situation in Russia Russian media has reported that a female researcher, identified as Darya Shipilova, 28, died after being exposed to the plague in a lab accident at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute. Initial reports said that Shipilova broke a test tube containing the plague bacteria Yersinia pestis in late September, came down with severe pneumonia and died of her illness. The World Health Organization said Shipilova died of severe pneumonia overnight into Oct. 2. Russian officials have since cast doubt on those reports. Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said there was no accident and that Shipilova had died of "pneumonia of unknown origin."
A maintenance worker walks out of the headquarters of Russia's consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, in Moscow on Oct. 5, 2026.
Igor Ivanko/AFP via Getty Images
The WHO said it was told by Russia on Oct. 6 that no plague was detected. The global health agency said it asked Russian authorities to provide information about which pathogen caused Shipilova's illness.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday called on Russia to be more transparent, and said the nation should "share more information with the world." The WHO said it is following the situation closely and requesting further information from Russian authorities. What is plague? Plague is caused by the Yersinia pestis bacteria. There are three main types of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.Bubonic plague is the most common form of plague. Infected people may have painfully swollen lymph nodes known as buboes, along with fever and chills, a severe headache, body aches and exhaustion. Septicemic plague happens when the Yersinia pestis bacteria enters the bloodstream. Patients may develop fever, chills, extreme weakness, abdominal pain, shock and possible internal bleeding. Some skin may turn black and die.
A microscopic image shows the Yersinia pestis bacteria, which causes plague infections in humans.
Ruslanas Baranuskas/Science Pho/Getty Images
Pneumonic plague typically occurs when the other forms of plague are not treated and the Yersinia pestis bacteria infects the lungs. Patients develop pneumonia and may show fever, headache, weakness, shortness of breath, chest pain, cough and bloody or watery mucus. The pneumonia could cause respiratory failure. This is considered the most serious version of plague, and is always fatal if left untreated. Russian media reports indicated that Shipilova may have died of pneumonic plague. How does plague spread? Plague is most commonly spread through the bite of fleas carried by infected rodents. Animals, including cats and dogs, can also become infected from eating smaller animals that were carrying those fleas.
Pneumonic plague can be spread between people. In cases of pneumonic plague, droplets emitted when a sick person coughs can lead to others becoming infected. Russia's health watchdog said that nearly 200 people who had come into contact with Shipilova before her death were tested, and none had plague.
This undated photo released in 2019 by the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East shows the institute workers in a lab.
The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East via AP
How is plague treated? Plague can be successfully treated with antibiotics, health organizations and doctors say. Patients need to be treated as soon as possible. Researchers who regularly work with plague can also be vaccinated for it, Gounder noted. Plague outbreaks in the Middle Ages killed millions, due to widespread, common flea and rat infestations and less understanding of how to prevent disease from spreading. About seven plague cases are reported each year in the United States, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. More than 80% of the cases in the U.S. are bubonic plague, the agency said.Most U.S. cases occur in the West and Southwest. Cases are usually treated successfully, according to CDC data. The last fatal case of plague in the U.S. was recorded in 2021.
Edited by
Nicole Brown Chau

sources.headline: US 'watching closely' after plague researcher dies in Russia
sources.text: President Donald Trump says the US is looking "very strongly" at the case of a Russian lab technician who died at a plague research centre in Siberia.Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was watching closely amid concerns the incident could lead to the spread of pneumonic plague, but there was no cause for alarm.Announcing the cause of death as "pneumonia of undetermined etiology", Irkutsk's governor said "no micro-organisms" linked to the woman's work had been found "in her biological samples".Unconfirmed reports suggested the woman fell ill either after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.Asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague spreading from Russia, Trump said he had not spoken to the Kremlin about it."I hate to see them having it," he said, but added: "We'll help. Everybody who has that kind of a problem, we'll always help."No other cases of staff from the plague institute seeking medical attention since the lab technician's death had been reported, Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev said, quoting Russia's consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor.The watchdog said a biological safety team had inspected the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk and found no emergency situation there.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged people not to "listen to various rumours" but "rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements" instead.Russian media reported last week that nearly 200 people known to have had contact with the dead woman were under medical observation as a precaution.Asked by a reporter for an "update on the suspected plague case in Russia", Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "It seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected and there's concern that that, you know, could have spread, at least internally - you've seen them do quarantine of this and that nature. "If something like that gets out, it can quickly spread. So we're watching and monitoring it closely. I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and the cause to just keep an eye on it and we're doing that."The woman who died, whose first name was given by Russian media as Daria and who was in her late twenties, had recently visited the Buryatia region on the border with Mongolia.The plague bacterium or Yersinia pestis, external, which killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death, is found among rodents such as marmots in the area. It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, external was founded just over 100 years ago.Dr Simon Clarke, an associate professor in cellular microbiology at the University of Reading, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the pneumonic version of Yersinia pestis was nearly always fatal if left untreated, but could be overcome with antibiotics. "Pneumonic plague can transmit from person to person and that is why there is the concern around this," he said. He added: "But of course people's thought with any outbreak of infectious disease at all runs to... lockdowns and Covid and that is just not what's going to happen here.""People think, 'Oh the plague, that's gone, that went hundreds of years ago,' but it hasn't," Clarke said. "It's still around and in certain parts of the world, it's a threat to human health and that's why they need to study it."Asked if the pathogen might have been studied for potential use as a bio-weapon, the scientist agreed it was possible."Because this is Russia people's thoughts are running to that, but I think my earlier explanation is probably more likely," Clarke said.According to the World Health Organization (WHO), pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal, if not diagnosed and treated early.People can be infected through:infected flea bitescontact with bodily fluids or contaminated materialsthe inhalation of respiratory particles.Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm.
